title: Unit 1.1 Self-Assessment
subtitle: Formal logic and set theory
intro: Every question below is drawn from a slide in the unit 1.1 deck, either stated there directly or a short step of reasoning away. Work through all of them, then submit to see your score alongside the justification for each answer.

questions.slide: The Role of Mathematics in Social Science Research
questions.prompt: The slides open by calling mathematics essential for social science. What reason do they give first?

options.text: It provides a precise language for defining and quantifying concepts such as probability, uncertainty and preferences
It guarantees that a theory's assumptions are empirically true
It removes the need to collect data
It makes research easier to publish

questions.explanation: The first bullet is headed 'Precision in Communication': mathematics gives a precise language to describe and analyse social phenomena, to quantify concepts like probability and preferences, and to be precise about what we mean when developing and testing theoretical claims.

questions.prompt: The slides offer the Prisoner's Dilemma as an example of which use of mathematics?
questions.explanation: It appears under 'Decision Making and Strategic Interaction', where game theory is offered as a framework for analysing strategic interaction. Regression is the example given for the separate 'Statistical Models' bullet.

questions.prompt: In the vocabulary given for proofs, which term names a result that is of little interest in itself and serves only as a stepping stone?
questions.explanation: The slides define a lemma as similar to a theorem but of little interest in and of itself, intended to be used only as a stepping stone.

questions.prompt: Which term is defined as a statement thought to be true given the assumptions made, but not yet proved?
questions.explanation: A proposition is thought to be true given the assumptions; once proved it becomes a theorem. An assumption is stated up front and taken to be true.

questions.prompt: 'If a number is an integer, then it is a rational number.' On the slides' reading, being rational is what for being an integer?
questions.explanation: A condition q is necessary for p if p cannot be true unless q is also true, written p ⇒ q. Integer ⇒ rational, so rationality is necessary for integrality. It is not sufficient: 1/2 is rational but not an integer.

questions.prompt: Given p ⇒ q, which of the following follow from the definition on the slides? Select all that apply.

options.text: p cannot be true unless q is also true
q cannot be true unless p is also true
p and q must always have the same truth value

questions.explanation: Both correct options restate the definition. The other two describe the converse q ⇒ p and the biconditional p ⇔ q, neither of which follows from p ⇒ q alone.

questions.prompt: 'A number is prime if and only if it has exactly two distinct positive divisors, 1 and itself.' This states a condition that is:
questions.explanation: 'If and only if' is the biconditional p ⇔ q, which the slides define as exactly the necessary-and-sufficient case. It gives a complete characterisation of primality.

questions.prompt: Every necessary condition is also a sufficient condition.
questions.explanation: Necessary is the single implication p ⇒ q. Sufficiency requires the other direction as well, and only together do they give p ⇔ q. Being rational is necessary for being an integer but not sufficient.

questions.slide: Why we need math (approaches to proofs)
questions.prompt: Which approaches to proof are listed on the slides? Select all that apply.

options.text: General deductive proof: assume p and show q

questions.explanation: The slide lists general deductive proof, proof by construction, proof by counterexample, proof by contradiction and proof by induction. Analogy and simulation are not among them.

questions.slide: Why we need math (approaches to proofs)
questions.prompt: To disprove a universal statement, which approach do the slides point to?
questions.explanation: Proof by counterexample is defined as giving a counterexample to disprove a universal statement. Proof by construction does the reverse: it gives an example to show something exists.

questions.slide: Why we need math (approaches to proofs)
questions.prompt: In proof by contradiction as the slides describe it, you assume ¬p and then show that ¬p implies:
questions.explanation: The slide states: if we want to prove p, assume ¬p is true and then prove that ¬p implies both q and ¬q. Deriving a statement and its negation is the contradiction.

questions.slide: Why we need math (approaches to proofs)
questions.prompt: The slides classify proof by induction as a non-deductive method of proof.
questions.explanation: The slide lists proof by induction and adds the parenthetical 'it is still deductive, though'.

questions.prompt: In the table of mathematical symbols, ∏ from i = k to l denotes:
questions.explanation: ∑ is the sum and ∏ is the product. The table lists both side by side.

questions.prompt: The table gives approximate values for two constants. Which pairing is right?
questions.explanation: The table lists π as approximately 3.14159 and Euler's number e as approximately 2.71828.

questions.prompt: Which symbol does the set theory table give for the Cartesian product of sets?
questions.explanation: × is the Cartesian product. ∪ is union, ∩ is intersection and \ is set difference.

questions.prompt: In set notation, the slides read the symbol | (or :) as:
questions.explanation: The table glosses | or : as 'such that', which is how it is used inside set-builder notation like {x ∈ ℕ | x is even}.

questions.prompt: According to the delimiters table, which brackets denote an open set?
questions.explanation: The table assigns { } to a discrete set, ( ) to an open set and [ ] to a closed set.

questions.prompt: Based on the logic notation table, select every correct reading.
questions.explanation: ⇒ means 'implies'; ⇔ means 'if and only if'. The other three readings are as listed.

questions.slide: Why Formal Logic? Two Pillars of Knowledge
questions.prompt: The slides pair each mode of reasoning with a core question. Which question belongs to rationalism?

options.text: What does the world show us?

questions.explanation: Rationalism is knowledge from reason and logical inference, asking what follows from our assumptions. Empiricism asks what the world shows us.

questions.slide: Why Formal Logic? Two Pillars of Knowledge
questions.prompt: The slides associate empiricism with the world of data, experiments and statistical evidence.
questions.explanation: That is the slide's description of empiricism: knowledge derived from observation and experience.

questions.slide: Why Formal Logic? The Bridge Between Theory and Data
questions.prompt: The slides say formal logic gives us the precise language needed to do which of the following? Select all that apply.

options.text: Formulate testable hypotheses that can be falsified
Guarantee that our premises are empirically true

questions.explanation: The three listed purposes are on the slide. Logic secures validity given the premises; whether the premises hold is an empirical question it cannot settle.

questions.slide: Why Formal Logic? The Bridge Between Theory and Data
questions.prompt: What distinguishes a scientific claim from a bare observation, on the slides' account?

options.text: It has a defined truth value, so it can be true or false
It has a large sample size
It specifies a domain of discourse

questions.explanation: The slide says a scientific claim is more than an observation: it is a statement with a defined truth value, which is what makes it falsifiable.

questions.prompt: How do the slides define a mathematical statement, or proposition?

options.text: A declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both
A sentence that is true, false, or undetermined
A sentence that is assumed true without proof

questions.explanation: That definition is what allows propositions to be combined with connectives and evaluated in truth tables.

questions.prompt: Under the definitions given, the implication p → q is false:

options.text: Only when p is true and q is false
Only when both p and q are false

questions.explanation: The slide states implication is false only when p is true and q is false. In all three other rows it is true, including both rows where p is false.

questions.prompt: Using the connective definitions on the slide, select every true statement.

options.text: ¬p is true when p is false
p ∧ q is true only when both are true
p ∨ q is true when at least one is true
p ↔ q is true only when both are true

questions.explanation: The biconditional is true when p and q are either both true or both false, so the last option omits the false-false case.

questions.prompt: For two propositions p and q, in how many of the four rows of the truth table is p ∧ q true?
questions.explanation: Only the row where p and q are both true gives p ∧ q = T; the other three rows are false.

questions.prompt: A truth table lists all possible truth values. For two propositions, how many rows does it need?
questions.explanation: Each proposition takes two values, so two propositions give 2² = 4 combinations, as in the conjunction table on the slide.

questions.prompt: The slides give which equivalence as their example?
questions.explanation: An implication fails only when p holds and q does not, which is exactly when ¬p ∨ q fails, so the two are equivalent.

questions.prompt: Two statements count as logically equivalent if they agree in at least one row of the truth table.
questions.explanation: The definition requires that they always have the same truth value, that is, in every row.

questions.prompt: Writing out the full truth table shows that p ↔ q is logically equivalent to:
questions.explanation: The two columns match in all four rows. This is why proving a biconditional means proving both directions.

questions.prompt: In the truth table for p ↔ q, which rows come out true?

options.text: The row where both are true and the row where both are false
Only the row where both are true
Only the rows where the two differ

questions.explanation: The biconditional holds exactly when the two propositions share a truth value, which is the top and bottom rows.

questions.prompt: By De Morgan's laws as stated for logic, ¬(p ∧ q) is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: Negating a conjunction flips it to a disjunction of the negations. The companion law is ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q.

questions.prompt: And ¬(p ∨ q) is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: Negating a disjunction flips it to a conjunction of the negations: neither p nor q holds.

questions.prompt: Using the slide's definitions and examples, select every true statement.

options.text: A tautology is a statement that is always false
A contradiction is true in at least one row of its truth table

questions.explanation: A contradiction is always false and a tautology always true; P ∧ ¬P and P ∨ ¬P are the slide's examples.

questions.prompt: How do the slides state the key difference between the two logics?

options.text: Propositional logic treats statements as indivisible, while predicate logic looks inside them and expresses structure with quantifiers
Predicate logic treats statements as indivisible, while propositional logic breaks them apart
Predicate logic has no logical connectives
Propositional logic is the one that uses ∀ and ∃

questions.explanation: Propositional logic's basic unit is the whole proposition; predicate logic breaks it into objects and properties and adds quantifiers.

questions.prompt: ∀x (Cat(x) → Mammal(x)) is offered as an example of:
questions.explanation: It quantifies over objects and applies predicates to them, which is exactly what propositional logic cannot do.

questions.prompt: The slides state that a negated universal, ¬∀, is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: ¬∀ is ∃¬ and ¬∃ is ∀¬. Saying 'not everything has the property' is saying 'something lacks it'.

questions.prompt: What does the quantifier ∃! mean?
questions.explanation: ∃ asserts existence of at least one element; ∃! is the unique existential quantifier, asserting exactly one.

questions.slide: Direct Proof Strategy Using Predicate Logic
questions.prompt: In the direct proof that n even implies n² even, the argument reaches n² = 2(2k²). Why does that finish the proof?

options.text: Because 2k² is an integer, n² has the form 2m required by the definition of even
Because 4k² is even for every k
Because k was assumed to be even
Because squaring always preserves parity by assumption

questions.explanation: The goal q was stated as '∃m ∈ ℤ : n² = 2m'. Writing n² as 2 times the integer 2k² exhibits that m, which is what had to be shown.

questions.prompt: How do the slides define an open sentence?

options.text: A predicate with free variables, not true or false until the variables are assigned or quantified
A proposition that is always true
A set written in set-builder notation
A declarative sentence containing no variables

questions.explanation: A predicate such as P(x): 'x is even' becomes a proposition only once x is specified, as in P(4), or once it is quantified.

questions.prompt: The 'domain of discourse' is:

options.text: The set of values over which a variable ranges
The set of true propositions in an argument
The set of quantifiers in use

questions.explanation: Quantifiers apply to predicates over this domain, which is what turns an open sentence into a proposition.

questions.slide: Proof by Contradiction Using Predicate Logic
questions.prompt: The proof that √2 is irrational begins by assuming that √2 is irrational.
questions.explanation: It begins by assuming the negation of the conclusion, that √2 is rational and so equals a/b for coprime integers a and b. The contradiction that follows is what establishes irrationality.

questions.slide: Proof by Contradiction Using Predicate Logic
questions.prompt: What is the contradiction that ends the √2 proof?

options.text: a and b both turn out to be even, contradicting that they were chosen coprime
a² turns out to be odd
b² turns out to be odd
The equation √2 = a/b has no solution in the integers

questions.explanation: From a² = 2b² the proof gets a even, writes a = 2k, and derives b² = 2k², so b is even too. Two coprime integers cannot share the factor 2.

questions.prompt: Inference rules are described as patterns that guarantee:

options.text: A true conclusion if the premises are true

questions.explanation: They are the scaffolding of a valid argument. Validity transmits truth from premises to conclusion; it does not certify the premises.

questions.slide: Valid Inference Rules in Propositional Logic
questions.prompt: Select every inference that is valid according to the rules on the slides.

options.text: From X and X → Y, conclude Y
From X ∨ Y and ¬X, conclude Y
From X → Y and Y, conclude X

questions.explanation: The first three are modus ponens, modus tollens and disjunctive syllogism. The last affirms the consequent, which is not among the valid rules: Y may hold for reasons other than X.

questions.slide: Valid Inference Rules in Propositional Logic
questions.prompt: From X → Y and Y → Z we may conclude X → Z. Which rule is this?
questions.explanation: The slides name it hypothetical syllogism and gloss it as transitivity, chaining two implications into one.

questions.slide: Modus Ponens as a Logical Formula
questions.prompt: Modus ponens can be written as the formula (X ∧ (X → Y)) → Y. What does its truth table show?

options.text: The final column is true in all four rows
The final column is true only when X is true
The final column is false in exactly one row
The final column matches the column for X → Y

questions.explanation: A tautology is true under every assignment, so all four rows of the last column read T. That is what makes modus ponens a rule rather than a contingent claim.

questions.slide: Valid Inference: The Logic of Scientific Claims
questions.prompt: Modus tollens is glossed as 'the way of denying'. With a theory P → Q, observing ¬Q licenses which conclusion?
questions.explanation: If the theory implies the effect and the effect is absent, the cause must have been absent too.

questions.slide: Inference Rules in a Social Psychology Experiment
questions.prompt: With hypothesis H₁: P → Q, assigning a subject to the treatment group establishes P. Predicting that they show Q uses which rule?
questions.explanation: The slide calls this the logic of the treatment group and the core of experimental prediction: from P → Q and P, infer Q.

questions.slide: Inference Rules in a Social Psychology Experiment
questions.prompt: According to the slides, what does it mean if a subject in the treatment group does not show individualistic behaviour?

options.text: It is evidence against the hypothesis
It tells us nothing either way

questions.explanation: The slide notes that ¬Q in a control subject lets us infer ¬P, confirming the manipulation, but that ¬Q in a treated subject is, more powerfully, evidence against the hypothesis itself.

questions.slide: Inference Rules in a Social Psychology Experiment
questions.prompt: Given P → Q (money prime causes individualism) and Q → R (individualism reduces help-seeking), what new testable hypothesis do the slides derive?
questions.explanation: Chaining the two implications by hypothetical syllogism yields P → R: priming with money will cause subjects to seek less help.

questions.prompt: What does the set-builder expression A = {x ∈ ℕ | x is even} denote?

options.text: The set of all even natural numbers
The set containing the single element 'x is even'
The natural numbers together with the even numbers
The set of all natural numbers

questions.explanation: Set-builder notation specifies the properties elements must satisfy: take x from ℕ, keep those that are even.

questions.prompt: The slides give a route to proving A = B. Which one?

options.text: Show A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A
Show A and B have the same number of elements

questions.explanation: Equality is ∀x (x ∈ A ⇔ x ∈ B), and the slide notes that if A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A then A = B. This double-inclusion strategy is exactly what the De Morgan proof later uses.

questions.prompt: Which formalisation of 'A is a subset of B' do the slides give?
questions.explanation: Subset is a one-directional implication. The biconditional version is set equality, and reversing the arrow gives B ⊆ A.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the special sets introduced.

options.text: ∅ is a subset of every set
A singleton set contains exactly one element
The universal set is a subset of every other set

questions.explanation: The relationship runs the other way for the universal set: all other sets are subsets of U, since it contains everything under consideration.

questions.prompt: If A = {1, 2}, how many elements does the power set ℘(A) have?
Using the definitions on the operations slide, select every correct one.

options.text: A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}
A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}
A \ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}

questions.explanation: The difference requires x ∈ A and x ∉ B. As written, that option describes the intersection instead.

questions.prompt: Which identity do the slides list under distributivity?
questions.explanation: The other three are, in order, associativity, commutativity and De Morgan's law, each listed separately on the same slide.

questions.prompt: De Morgan's laws for sets state that (A ∩ B)ᶜ equals:
questions.explanation: Complementing an intersection turns it into a union of complements, mirroring ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q in logic.

questions.slide: Proof of De Morgan's Law for Sets
questions.prompt: How does the proof of (A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ establish the equality?

options.text: By showing each side is a subset of the other
By induction on the size of A

questions.explanation: It takes an arbitrary x in the left side and derives membership in the right, giving one inclusion, then runs the argument in reverse for the other. Two inclusions give equality.

questions.prompt: Select every accurate description from the number sets slide.

options.text: ℕ is the positive integers from 1 upwards, sometimes including 0
ℤ is all positive and negative whole numbers, including zero
ℝ covers all decimal values, rational and irrational alike
ℂ consists of numbers a + bi where i² = 1

questions.explanation: Complex numbers are defined with i² = −1, not +1. The other three match the slide.

questions.prompt: Which set is defined as the numbers expressible as a fraction a/b?
questions.explanation: That definition is what makes 'being rational' a necessary condition for 'being an integer' in the earlier example: every integer n is n/1.

questions.prompt: In the set-theoretic treatment of probability, the sample space S is:

options.text: The set of all possible outcomes of the experiment
A single outcome of the experiment
The set of outcomes we happen to observe
The probability assigned to an outcome

questions.explanation: For a coin toss S = {Heads, Tails}, and the event 'getting Heads' is the subset E = {Heads}.

questions.prompt: Which set-theoretic object does the sample space play the role of?
questions.explanation: The slide says S is a universal set in the context of a probabilistic experiment, which is why every event, as a subset of S, is well defined.

questions.prompt: An event is defined as:

options.text: Any subset of the sample space
Any element of the sample space
Any set containing the sample space
Any set disjoint from the sample space

questions.explanation: For a die roll, E₁ = {2, 4, 6} and E₂ = {1, 2, 3} are events precisely because they are subsets of S = {1,...,6}.

questions.prompt: A die is rolled, so the sample space is S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Let A be the event 'the roll is less than 4', A = {1, 2, 3}, and B the event 'the roll is even', B = {2, 4, 6}. Select every correct result.
questions.explanation: A ∪ B is every outcome that is under 4 or even. Only 5 is neither, so it is the single face left out. A ∩ B is the outcomes that are both, and 2 is the one roll under 4 that is also even.

questions.prompt: Rolling an even number, A = {2,4,6}, and rolling an odd number, B = {1,3,5}, are mutually exclusive. What makes them so?

options.text: A and B have the same number of elements

questions.explanation: Mutual exclusivity is empty intersection: the events cannot occur together on a single roll. Here Aᶜ does happen to equal B, but that is exhaustiveness rather than the definition of exclusivity.

questions.prompt: With strategy set S = {C, D} for each of two prisoners, how many strategy profiles does S₁ × S₂ contain?
questions.explanation: The Cartesian product pairs each of 2 strategies with each of 2 others: {(C,C), (C,D), (D,C), (D,D)}.

questions.prompt: In the strategy profile (D, C), both prisoners defect.
questions.explanation: Ordered pairs carry the players' identities: (D, C) means prisoner 1 defects while prisoner 2 cooperates. Both defecting is (D, D).
